correctness.rationale: The proof treats every distinct-prime competitor with product at most \(qM\). Removing its maximum prime gives \(R<4M^2\) via the product-versus-cardinality bound, and \(q(R-M)\le R(u-d)\). Since \(q>16M^4\), \(R>M\) is impossible; \(R=M\) forces the original set by unique factorization, and \(R<M\) yields a prime at a finite nonzero even offset. Conversely, every such prime offset creates a distinct-prime set of the same sum with smaller product. The analytic count invokes the known unconditional Selberg sieve bound for each nonzero fixed even shift. A separately executed dynamic-programming computation verifies 867 small exact-sum prime extensions for four bases, with explicit recognition that it is not an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The closest originating paper proves only existence through isolated primes and explicitly asks for the growth of admissible extension primes. The present central claim is a complete eventual necessary-and-sufficient characterization by finitely many computable shifted-prime obstructions. value.rationale: The finite obstruction Δ_A, computable independently of q, exactly classifies all sufficiently large prime extensions of every fixed minimum-product distinct-prime partition. This natural structural criterion resolves an explicitly posed extension-prime question, strengthens a nonconstructive existence lemma to a necessary-and-sufficient arithmetic test, and gives the unconditional π(X)+O_A(X/log²X) count and \(q_A(n)\sim n\log n\). The new mathematical value resides especially in the inverse characterization rather than the already suggested density-one consequence.
